query: Consider the following context: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered promising candidate materials for next‐generation nuclear reactors due to their superior mechanical strength, irradiation resistance, and thermal stability at high temperatures. However, the significant positive heat of mixing between refractory alloying elements and Cu, commonly used in cooling systems, poses challenges in forming composite structures. In that context, which method can be used for large‐scale reaction and stable microstructure, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing spark plasma sintering (SPS) processing parameters using a data‐driven approach will mitigate the detrimental effects of the high positive heat of mixing between the refractory elements and Cu, resulting in a homogeneous and stable composite microstructure on a large scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A mixed powder precursor composed of refractory high‐entropy alloy elements and Cu that naturally tends to segregate due to a high positive heat of mixing.
generation.intervention: Apply spark plasma sintering with systematically optimized parameters (heating rate, applied pressure, and dwell time) determined via a data‐driven or machine learning framework.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sintering conditions under rapid heating and high pressure, mimicking conditions relevant for next‐generation nuclear reactor structural components.
generation.structural_mediator: Rapid densification and kinetic suppression of phase segregation during SPS.
generation.mechanism: The fast heating, high pressure, and short dwell time enabled by SPS delay diffusional processes that lead to Cu segregation; data‐driven optimization further refines these parameters to ensure uniform reaction kinetics and a stable microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: A composite structure with minimal Cu segregation, exhibiting improved microstructural homogeneity and stability, which should translate into superior high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: Conventional reactive sintering or melting techniques that do not adequately control the reaction kinetics, leading to phase segregation and inhomogeneous microstructures in the RHEA-Cu composites.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis may not hold if scale‐up introduces uncontrolled thermal gradients or if the optimized parameters vary significantly with changes in powder morphology or composition.
generation.uncertainty: While SPS has shown promise at the lab scale, the exact optimized parameter window for large-scale production and its consistency across various alloy compositions remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled experiment using RHEA-Cu composite powders processed under traditional sintering conditions versus SPS with data‐driven optimized parameters. Systematically vary the SPS process parameters (heating rate, pressure, dwell time) using a full factorial design. Characterize the resulting microstructures and mechanical properties.
measurements: Microstructural uniformity and phase distribution via SEM and TEM
Elemental mapping to assess Cu segregation via EDS
Mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength) at high temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RHEA-Cu composites processed with data‐driven optimized SPS parameters do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in microstructural homogeneity and reduced Cu segregation compared to conventional processing, or if the mechanical performance does not improve correspondingly, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: According to the traditional alloy design theory, ordered phases or intermetallic compounds will form as the number of alloying elements increases. However, Yeh et al. observes that simple solid solution phases, instead of intermetallic compounds, are formed in an equiatomic quinary alloy. Subsequently, they propose a new alloy system, termed high entropy alloys (HEAs), which contain at least five principal elements, each having the atomic percentage between 5% and 35% [ [1] , [2] ]. Since the development of HEAs, a substantial number of studies on HEA have been performed. Some of these studies are focused on alloys comprised of elements with low melting points, such as AlCoCrCuFeNi system alloys [ [3] , [4] ], commonly exhibiting high ductility and low strength. On the other hand, refractory HEAs have exhibited advantages of high yield strength at room and elevated temperature. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. decision.trend: Early work on refractory high‐entropy alloys employed traditional melting and mechanical alloying approaches, but they struggled with phase segregation and inhomogeneous microstructures—especially when reactive elements with high positive heats of mixing (such as Cu) were incorporated. More recent studies demonstrated that spark plasma sintering (SPS), with its rapid heating rates, high pressures, and very short dwell times, can kinetically suppress segregation and enable a more uniform reaction even in systems prone to unfavorable mixing. However, while these SPS‐based routes have improved microstructural stability at a lab scale, scaling them up and fine‐tuning the reaction kinetics to overcome the specific challenge of integrating Cu with refractory elements remains an open issue.
decision.unsolved: How to control and optimize the reaction kinetics at large scale so that the significant positive heat of mixing between refractory alloying elements and Cu does not lead to phase segregation and undermines the composite stability.
decision.why: Recent trends show that SPS is effective in rapidly achieving a stable microstructure by overcoming unfavorable mixing in RHEAs. However, due to the complex interplay of heating rate, pressure, and dwell time needed to mitigate Cu segregation, a data‐driven or machine learning approach is the most plausible next step. Such a method can systematically analyze and optimize SPS parameters for large‐scale processing, ensuring that the reaction kinetics are precisely controlled to achieve homogeneous, stable composite structures.
